raw_text:
### Cardiac amyloidosis

Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded amyloid fibrils, most commonly immunoglobulin light chain (AL) or transthyretin (ATTR) amyloid [1]. Misfolding, oligomer toxicity, and progressive interstitial expansion produce restrictive physiology, atrial myopathy, conduction disease, and heart failure, often with preserved ejection fraction until late disease [2]. AL amyloidosis arises from a clonal plasma-cell disorder and is a hematologic emergency because circulating light chains are directly cardiotoxic and untreated advanced cardiac involvement may progress rapidly [3]. ATTR cardiomyopathy results from deposition of wild-type transthyretin, typically in older adults, or variant transthyretin due to pathogenic TTR mutations [4,5]. Recognition has increased because ATTR is found in a meaningful subset of older patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and in patients with aortic stenosis undergoing valve replacement [6,7]. The Val122Ile variant, now commonly termed p.Val142Ile, is particularly relevant in people of African ancestry and can present as late-onset cardiomyopathy [8]. Occult ATTR in calcific aortic stenosis is clinically important because dual pathology may worsen symptoms and outcomes [9].

Diagnosis begins with suspicion. “Red flags” include unexplained increased left ventricular wall thickness, discordant low QRS voltage or pseudo-infarct patterns, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, autonomic dysfunction, nephrotic-range proteinuria, biceps tendon rupture, atrial arrhythmias, and intolerance of standard heart-failure vasodilators [10,11]. Once suspected, testing should proceed in parallel to establish amyloid type. Tissue confirmation with Congo red staining remains definitive, and mass spectrometry is preferred for amyloid typing when available [12]. Echocardiography typically shows increased wall thickness, biatrial enlargement, diastolic dysfunction, valve thickening, pericardial effusion, and impaired longitudinal strain with relative apical sparing [13]. Cardiac magnetic resonance demonstrates diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal gadolinium kinetics, and increased extracellular volume; these features are diagnostically and prognostically informative [14,15]. Bone-avid radionuclide scintigraphy with technetium-labeled pyrophosphate, DPD, or HMDP has transformed ATTR diagnosis [16]. In patients with grade 2–3 myocardial uptake and no monoclonal protein by serum free-light-chain assay plus serum and urine immunofixation, ATTR cardiomyopathy can be diagnosed noninvasively without endomyocardial biopsy [17]. Conversely, any monoclonal protein requires careful evaluation for AL amyloidosis, because ATTR and monoclonal gammopathy can coexist.

Risk stratification is biomarker-driven. In AL amyloidosis, troponin and natriuretic peptides define cardiac stage and are powerful predictors of early mortality [18]. The revised Mayo system adds the difference between involved and uninvolved free light chains, integrating plasma-cell burden with cardiac injury [19]. In ATTR, natriuretic peptides, troponin, renal function, functional capacity, and imaging burden predict survival; staging systems for wild-type and broader ATTR cohorts help guide prognosis and trial design [20,21]. Atrial mechanical dysfunction is common, and intracardiac thrombus may occur even in sinus rhythm, so anticoagulation decisions should consider atrial arrhythmia, atrial mechanical failure, and bleeding risk rather than rhythm alone [22].

Management combines amyloid-directed therapy with meticulous cardiovascular care. Diuretics remain the cornerstone for congestion, but excessive preload reduction can precipitate hypotension; beta-blockers, renin–angiotensin system inhibitors, and nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers are often poorly tolerated. AL therapy aims for rapid, deep hematologic response. Daratumumab added to cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone has improved hematologic and organ responses in newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis [23]. Response assessment relies on free-light-chain reduction and cardiac biomarkers, because early falls in NT-proBNP predict improved survival [24]. Selected patients may be candidates for autologous stem-cell transplantation, advanced heart-failure therapies, or sequential heart transplantation and plasma-cell-directed therapy, but these decisions require specialized centers.

ATTR therapy now includes both stabilizers and silencers. Tafamidis reduced mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in ATTR cardiomyopathy and established TTR stabilization as disease-modifying treatment [25]. Acoramidis, another stabilizer designed for near-complete TTR stabilization, improved hierarchical clinical outcomes in ATTR-CM [26]. RNA-interference therapy has expanded the field: patisiran improved functional capacity and quality of life over 12 months [27], and vutrisiran reduced death and recurrent cardiovascular events in HELIOS-B [28]. Gene-editing approaches are investigational but may enable durable TTR reduction after one infusion; early studies of CRISPR-Cas9 editing in ATTR and specifically ATTR cardiomyopathy showed substantial TTR lowering, although long-term safety and clinical efficacy remain under study [29,30]. Overall, cardiac amyloidosis has shifted from a frequently missed, fatal diagnosis to a treatable cardiomyopathy, provided clinicians identify it early, type amyloid accurately, and initiate subtype-specific therapy promptly.
